title: Crash points anchored to message dispatch events
description: Add an opt-in explorer config field crash_after_send_probability (default 0.0). When a generated plan contains a Crash event for node N that is dependency-eligible, and the scheduler observes node N dispatch a remote message, with probability p immediately prioritize that Crash runnable (boost its selection score to ~1.0 for the next few steps). Implement in spur-core/src/simulator/core/scheduler.rs score path + a small state hook where dispatches are recorded; thread config through ExplorerConfig -> SingleRunConfig -> scheduler state. Enable at 0.3 in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json.
rationale: The oracle bug (and many crash-recovery protocol bugs) requires a node to crash in the narrow window after sending a message and before its delivery. Random crash placement almost never lands there; H1 hazard rate is ~28% per run but the crash rarely hits the critical sender.
generalityArgument: Anchors crashes to a universal protocol event (any remote send by any node), no function names or protocol structure involved.

title: Hold in-flight messages of a crashed sender until it recovers
description: Add opt-in config field orphan_hold_probability (default 0.0). When a node crashes while messages it dispatched are still undelivered, with probability p per message move those messages into purgatory with release scheduled at/after the sender's Recover event (or a bounded delay if it never recovers). Implement alongside the existing purgatory in core/exec.rs + scheduler crash path (crash_node already walks queues). Enable at 0.5 in general_vr.json.
rationale: Directly manufactures the H2 stale-incarnation hazard: a message from a dead incarnation delivered after the node is back. H2 measured at ~19-26% incidentally; making it deliberate should sharply lift P(depth>=5..7) where the oracle chain needs pre-crash StartViewChange-class messages delivered post-recovery.
generalityArgument: Purely about crash/dispatch/delivery timing relationships; applies to every message type on every protocol.

title: Turn on message-delay purgatory in the general config
description: Set purgatory: {delay_probability: 0.15, delay_duration_range: [5, 100]} in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json. No Rust changes.
rationale: Purgatory exists but is disabled by default and the loop config never enables it; delayed messages are a precondition for several oracle chain links (old messages arriving after recovery).
generalityArgument: Config-only, protocol-agnostic delay mechanism that already exists.

title: Turn on timeline feedback + steer in the general config
description: Set feedback: {mode: "timeline", steer: true} in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json. No Rust changes. Measure ladder + utilization (steer divergent picks) vs baseline.
rationale: The feedback/steer machinery exists but the loop's general config runs feedback off; the utilization counters show whether steer actually changes decisions, and the ladder shows whether that helps.
generalityArgument: Existing generic novelty mechanism; no protocol knowledge.

title: Remove the dead randomly_drop_msgs code path
description: The schedule_runnable parameter randomly_drop_msgs is hardwired false at both call sites; the 30% drop branch is dead code. Remove the parameter and branch (flag-off stage is trivially satisfied since it is already off). Non-inferiority expected to be exact.
rationale: Dead code in the scheduler hot path is noise for every future hypothesis; removing it is free simplification and validates the ablation pipeline end to end.
generalityArgument: Removes nothing observable; pure code hygiene.

title: Incarnation-aware timeline novelty tuples
description: Track a per-node incarnation counter (increments on Recover) in run state. Extend TimelineTuple (feedback.rs) with a small incarnation-crossing flag: whether the delivered message was dispatched in an earlier incarnation of the sender or delivered to a node in a later incarnation than at dispatch time. Behind config field incarnation_novelty: bool (default false). With steer on, novel crossing tuples get chased automatically.
rationale: Post-recovery deliveries of pre-crash messages are exactly the transitions the oracle chain needs (links 4-7); making them first-class novelty targets lets existing steer machinery hunt them.
generalityArgument: Incarnation counting is protocol-independent (crash/recover are simulator events).

title: Fire timers on at most one node per window
description: Add queue-policy option timer_exclusive: bool (default false): when the timer queue is selected, prefer timers belonging to a single 'active timeout node' chosen per window (e.g. rotate every K steps), instead of any node's timer. Implement as a wrapper in core/queue_selector.rs. Enable in general_vr.json.
rationale: The oracle scenario needs exactly one backup to time out (starting a view change) while others stay quiet; when all backups race, view changes trample each other and the single-suspect pattern almost never occurs.
generalityArgument: One-suspect-at-a-time is a generic failure-detector pattern, not a VR concept.

title: PCT-style priority change points selector
description: Add within_queue_selector variant {type: "Pct", depth: d}: assign random static priorities to runnables and at d random steps during the run demote the currently-highest class (classic probabilistic concurrency testing). Implement in core/queue_selector.rs behind the existing selector enum; default remains Tournament. Try depth 3-8 in general_vr.json.
rationale: PCT gives provable lower bounds on hitting bugs of small depth; the oracle bug's depth may be within reach where uniform random is hopeless.
generalityArgument: PCT is a general-purpose concurrency testing algorithm.

title: Use hazard events as fitness for genetic/AOS modes
description: Count H1/H2-style hazard events in-run (sender-crash-with-inflight, post-recovery delivery of pre-crash message — the simulator knows dispatch/crash/recover/delivery ordering) into cheap per-run counters; add feedback mode "hazard" (or blend weight) so plan_score rewards runs that manufacture hazards. Behind config; default off. Then run genetic/AOS with hazard fitness in a variant general config.
rationale: Timeline novelty rewards any new ordering; hazard fitness rewards exactly the crash-recovery races the ladder measures, closing the loop between grading and searching without leaking the oracle.
generalityArgument: Hazard definitions reference only simulator-level events (dispatch, crash, recover, deliver).

title: Reduce explorer allocation/clone traffic (Arc/imbl memmove)
description: The perf profile shows 26.5% of cycles in memmove from Arc::make_mut and imbl persistent-vector promote/push on the hot execution path. Reduce allocation/clone traffic: avoid make_mut on shared values that are then dropped, small-value inlining, reuse per-run buffers. Note: measured explorer peak RSS is only ~2.4G on a 13.5k-run session — memory is NOT the explorer's problem (the grader was); this is a throughput hypothesis, verified by the A/B bench.
rationale: The same clone traffic dominates CPU; cutting it is the most direct throughput win the profile offers.
generalityArgument: Pure implementation efficiency; no scheduling semantics involved.

title: Size the send-delay hold to the graded workload's run length
description: In scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json change purgatory.delay_duration_range from [5, 100] to [5, 1000]. No code change and no new field; the value is a config-only recalibration of a mechanism that is already on. Classified as enabling because the current cap makes the mechanism unreachable for the rungs it exists to serve, not because the path is dead. exec.rs draws the hold log-uniformly over the range and sets release_step = current_step + duration, so the range is measured in scheduler steps. Over [5, 100] the median draw is 22 steps and the maximum is 100. Over [5, 1000] the median is 71 and 31% of draws exceed 192, while the cap stays below the 2387-step mean run length so delayed records still deliver before the run ends.
rationale: The graded chain needs two StartViewChange messages sent before the first crash to be delivered after a second write that follows the second recovery. Measured on the general grid, that span is median 192 steps and p90 338, against median 25 and p90 35 in findbug_archive where the bug is found. The send delay is the only mechanism that holds a message that long: the runnable set has median size 4 in both corpora, so a record surviving 192 steps unselected has probability near 1e-19. The current maximum hold of 100 steps sits below the median requirement, so no draw can bridge it in more than half of correctly shaped runs. The fault schedule itself is not the shortfall - the general grid already produces the full findbug fault shape about 125 times per 54k chunk and still records zero violations. The ladder points at the same place: depthAtLeast over a 54000-run chunk is [54000, 49420, 35424, 19045, 4446, 719, 90, 5], so per-rung survival is 0.92, 0.72, 0.54, 0.23, 0.16, 0.13, 0.06. The two worst rungs are the write after both recoveries and the delivery of the pre-crash messages after it, while the rung that only has to cross a single crash survives at 0.54. Short holds pass and long holds do not.
generalityArgument: Changes one number in a delivery-delay range. It names no handler, node, or protocol, and the argument for it is that a hold window should scale with the run length of the workload being explored, which is true of any protocol under any spec.
notes: Falsifier: if depth>=7 and depth>=8 counts do not rise while purgatory delayed-send counters stay comparable, the hold length is not the binding constraint and the send-delay family should be closed rather than tuned further. Watch runsPerSec and iterations_exhausted for the cost side.

title: Prefer firing a node's timer when that node has no other queued work
description: In spur-core/src/simulator/core/scheduler.rs, extend score_runnable with a third structural case alongside the existing quick-fire branch. A Runnable::Timer whose node has an empty local queue is 'starved'; reweight its score against a new config field timer_starvation_multiplier exactly as quick_fire_multiplier reweights a Recover whose node is crashed. Default the field to 1.0 so today's behavior is unchanged, add it to EXPLORER_CONFIG_KEYS, and enable it at a value above 1 in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json. score_runnable currently receives only currently_crashed, so the node's local queue length has to be threaded in alongside it; that is the bulk of the work. Add util_stats counters timer_admission.{offered, starved_offered, fired_starved, fired_busy} so the mechanism counts its own firing.
rationale: Timer admission is the difference the goal document names as the largest unexplained gap: the plan corpora violate at 76% at depth 8 against under 1.8% for the general grid, the plans decide when timers may fire, and the general grid lets the simulator fire them at will. That capability is missing rather than mis-tuned - strict_timers is a PlanConfig field, absent from EXPLORER_CONFIG_KEYS, and timer_gate_blocks gates on allowed_timers which only plan AllowTimer events populate. This is also the only shape of intervention that can reach the decision at all: score_runnable is 0.25*novelty + 0.75*priority, priority is a random draw taken at runnable creation, and novelty saturates after two to three hundred runs, so a term weighted 0.25 cannot outvote a coin flip weighted 0.75. The quick-fire branch is the one place the scorer overrides that randomness, and it does so structurally rather than through novelty. That is why timer-vs-delivery-coverage-axis failed and why this is not the same proposal.
generalityArgument: The rule stated without reference to the protocol under test: prefer firing a node's timer when that node has no other work queued. It names no handler, message, timer label or role. A timeout is a statement about the absence of expected input, so firing one while the node still has queued input models a spurious timeout that any protocol is built to absorb, while firing one into a genuinely starved node is the case the recovery path exists for. The same quiescence effect is measured on the crash side: every crash in findbug_archive lands with zero client operations outstanding against 9.3% on the general grid.
notes: Falsifier: if timer_admission.fired_starved does not rise relative to fired_busy, the multiplier is not reaching the decision and the mechanism is miswired rather than unhelpful - fix the wiring before reading any ladder number. Priced at 4 because it needs a new config key and a new argument threaded into score_runnable, per the goal document's rule that a probe is priced by what it has to add. Expect the effect at depth>=4, the only rung stable to a tenth of a percent; depth>=6 moves 7.5% on a null diff.

title: Guarantee some client work is scheduled after every fault
description: In spur-core/src/simulator/path/generator.rs, add an opt-in generator field post_fault_client_ops (default 0, preserving today's plans). When set to k >= 1, after the write-chain pass and before the probabilistic dependency pass, for each crash/recover pair add a mandatory edge from its RecoverNode node to k client-request nodes chosen at random from those not already reachable from that recover, skipping any edge that would close a cycle (the existing has_path_connecting guard). Thread the field through GeneratorConfig and ExplorerConfig, add it to EXPLORER_CONFIG_KEYS, and enable it at 1 in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json. Add util_stats counters post_fault_ops.{pairs_seen, edges_added, ops_invoked_after_last_recover} so the mechanism counts its own firing.
rationale: Measured on 30,024 general-config runs: 4,909 have two distinct nodes crash and recover, and in 3,880 of them (79%) every write is invoked before the first crash, so no write remains to be issued afterwards. Only 428 (8.7%) invoke a write after both recoveries and 176 (3.6%) complete one, while 3,458 (70%) have a write issued before the crash that never answers. The oracle chain is a write, then faults, then a second write, so four runs in five cannot express it for want of a second write. The cause is arithmetic rather than generator declaration order - generate_plan shuffles the node list before the probabilistic dependency pass - six to twelve client requests become eligible at once against one to three crashes, so every invocation has been issued by the time a crash is selected, and nothing guarantees client work survives a fault.
generalityArgument: The rule without reference to the protocol under test: every injected fault should have client work scheduled after it. It names no handler, message, timer label or role, and it is a property any fault-injection framework wants, since a fault whose effects no later operation observes cannot be detected by any oracle.
notes: Falsifier: if post_fault_ops.ops_invoked_after_last_recover does not rise, the edges are not reaching plan execution and the mechanism is miswired rather than unhelpful. Watch unpairedFraction, which should fall if stalled writes are replaced by completing ones, and expect a throughput cost since surviving client work lengthens runs. Judge the effect at depth>=4, the only rung stable to a tenth of a percent; depth>=6 moves 7.5% on a null diff. Note that P(depth>=k) mixes two populations, since roughly half of runs contain no write addressed to node 0 and are scored on a chain anchored at the first crash instead, so a mechanism that shifts that proportion moves the ladder for a reason unrelated to its mechanism.

title: End a stalled run and spend its remaining budget on a new one
description: In spur-core/src/simulator/path.rs, track per run the last step at which any node's state token (State::node_state_token) changed or a client operation was invoked or answered. Keep, per session in the feedback store, the longest such quiet stretch observed in any run that later completed. Behind an opt-in config field stall_abort (default false, today's semantics), end a run whose current quiet stretch exceeds that session-derived length with a new end_reason 'stalled' in the runs table, treating it like iterations_exhausted for grading. The threshold is the session's own distribution, not a constant, and it starts unset so the first completed run sets it. Add util_stats counters termination.stall_aborts and termination.steps_reclaimed (steps the aborted runs would still have spent), so the mechanism counts its own firing. Enable it in scheduler_configs/loop/general_vr.json.
rationale: research/observations/TERMINATION_DEPTH.md: on a 229,980-run general chunk, runs that complete reach depth>=6 at 0.094 against 0.016 for runs that exhaust the step budget (5.8x, z 87) and depth>=8 at 8.5x, with deep runs ending at a median of about 1,100 steps against the full 6,000 for exhausted ones; in the plan corpus all 11 violating runs are among the 103 of 3,000 that complete, finishing in about 100 steps while the rest burn 10,000. About 97% of the plan corpus's budget and roughly 70% of the general chunk's went to runs that had stopped progressing. Ending those runs early turns their steps into new runs, which is events per explore-second by construction if per-run depth holds.
generalityArgument: A stall is defined by the absence of any state change on any node, which any protocol exhibits and none names; the threshold is derived from the session's completed runs rather than chosen. No handler, message, role or timer label appears in the rule.
notes: The per-run depth guards must hold: a run that is cut before its plan's later operations can be issued reads shallower, so the mechanism is expected to raise events per second without lowering per-run depth, and a per-run decline is the falsifier.

title: Lower timer admission at a node whose idle firings change nothing
description: Using the timer effectiveness counters (util_stats timer_effects, keyed by resume vertex, whether a delivery to the node was in flight, incarnation and inert streak), keep per session in the feedback store a Beta(fired, acted) per key, and per node within a run the count for the same key. In score_runnable, behind an opt-in config field timer_effect_steer (default false), apply a multiplier that lowers the priority of admitting another timer at a (node, resume vertex) whose firings with no delivery in flight have been inert against the session's distribution for that key, and never lowers - optionally raises - a firing with a delivery in flight. The multiplier reorders and never zeroes a choice. Add util_stats counters timer_steer.{evaluated, lowered, raised}.
rationale: research/observations/TERMINATION_DEPTH.md shows depth and violations concentrated in the runs that complete and the budget spent on runs that stall; GOAL.md names timer admission relative to delivery as the variable the plan corpora constrain (76% violation at full depth under admitted timers against under 2% in general mode). Whether the stalled runs are dominated by inert timer firings on idle nodes is what the timer effectiveness join measures; this hypothesis is the runtime use of that measurement and is only worth running once the join says idle inert firings predict budget exhaustion.
generalityArgument: The rule names no handler, message or label: it keys on the CFG vertex a timer wakes, on whether a delivery is pending for the node, and on the node's own recent effect history, and the threshold is the session's distribution rather than a constant. A protocol whose timers act is left alone by construction.
notes: Keep firings with a delivery in flight unpenalised: that is the race the oracle chain needs, and it is often inert on average. Measure the base rate of the gating predicate (idle and inert) before building, per GOAL.md rule 8.
